narration.ref_text: Hello students, welcome back! Today we'll make judicial review super simple, so let's begin.
pieces: In nineteen seventy, new state laws threatened a quiet Kerala monastery.
Nobody imagined this local dispute would protect the Indian Constitution.
Welcome to our study of Kesavananda Bharati versus State of Kerala, decided on twenty-fourth April nineteen seventy-three by the Supreme Court.
This historic constitutional dispute was heard by a thirteen-judge Constitution Bench, which remains the largest bench ever assembled in Indian history.
By a razor-thin majority of seven to six, the judges placed a permanent limit on Parliament's power to amend the Indian Constitution.
To understand how a quiet monastery's land dispute gave birth to the basic structure doctrine, let us travel back to nineteen seventy.
Swami Kesavananda Bharati headed the Edneer Mutt in Kerala.
New state land reform laws suddenly restricted his monastery's property rights.
He approached the Supreme Court under Article 32.
He claimed the state laws violated his fundamental rights to religion and property.
While his petition was pending, Parliament stepped in and changed the rules.
New constitutional amendments shielded those Kerala laws from courts.
The Twenty-ninth Amendment placed the Kerala laws into the Ninth Schedule.
The Twenty-fourth and Twenty-fifth Amendments also expanded Parliament's power greatly.
Suddenly, the Mutt's right under Article 26 to manage its property turned into a fierce battle over Parliament's power to rewrite India's fundamental law.
The Twenty-fourth Amendment altered Article 368 to declare that Parliament could amend any provision freely without facing limits from Article 13.
The Twenty-fifth Amendment inserted Article 31C, which prevented courts from reviewing laws that claimed to implement Directive Principles of State Policy.
Therefore, the Supreme Court faced one monumental legal question: is Parliament's amending power under Article 368 unlimited, or are some boundaries unbreakable?
Because earlier rulings clashed on this question, the Supreme Court formed a thirteen-judge bench.
Never before had so many judges sat together.
To grasp the intense tension in nineteen seventy-three, we must trace twenty years of constitutional conflict between Parliament and the courts.
In nineteen fifty-one, in Shankari Prasad versus Union of India, the Court ruled that constitutional amendments are not ordinary laws under Article 13.
In nineteen sixty-five, Sajjan Singh versus State of Rajasthan repeated that view, though two judges warned that basic features might remain protected.
In nineteen sixty-seven, Golaknath reversed course by six to five, and in nineteen seventy-one Parliament hit back with the Twenty-fourth Amendment.
Furious over the Golaknath ruling, Parliament passed the Twenty-fourth Amendment in nineteen seventy-one.
It claimed full power to alter any Fundamental Right.
Now the thirteen judges had to decide whether Golaknath was right.
Could Parliament rewrite even the soul of the Constitution?
Hearings began on thirty-first October nineteen seventy-two.
They lasted sixty-eight working days, becoming one of the longest hearings in Supreme Court history.
Nani Palkhivala argued for the petitioners for thirty-one days.
He warned that unlimited amending power would destroy Indian democracy.
He argued that the word amend means to improve or adjust.
It cannot mean wiping out the essential features of the Constitution.
Parliament was created by the Constitution, he told the judges.
A creature of the Constitution cannot destroy its own creator.
The government counsel fiercely opposed any implied limits on Article 368.
He argued that Parliament represents the sovereign will of the people.
Without broad amending power, the state argued, socio-economic reforms would stall.
Future generations should not be chained forever to past legal rules.
Here stood the deepest conflict in Indian constitutional law, pulling two vital principles of democratic governance in completely opposite directions.
If Article 368 carried no limits whatsoever, a temporary parliamentary majority could abolish free elections, silence courts, or erase Fundamental Rights.
On the other hand, if Golaknath remained untouched, Parliament could never adjust Fundamental Rights even to pass urgent land and social reforms.
The thirteen judges needed a wise middle path: a basic structure that no parliamentary majority could ever touch.
For weeks after the hearings ended, the thirteen judges worked on separate opinions.
The bench was deeply divided right down the middle.
Six judges leaned firmly toward broad parliamentary amending power.
Six other judges insisted that Fundamental Rights could never be curtailed.
On twenty-fourth April nineteen seventy-three, the courtroom was packed to capacity.
Eleven separate opinions running over seven hundred pages were delivered.
Justice Hans Raj Khanna's opinion held the crucial deciding vote.
He rejected Golaknath, yet created a vital safeguard for the Constitution.
First, the thirteen-judge bench overruled Golaknath and upheld the Twenty-fourth Amendment, confirming that Parliament can indeed amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368.
Second, by seven to six, the Court declared that the power to amend does not include the power to destroy the basic structure.
Features like constitutional supremacy, republican democracy, secularism, separation of powers, and federalism were highlighted by various judges as part of this core identity.
Third, while upholding the Twenty-ninth Amendment, the Court struck down the second part of Article 31C that tried to block judicial review.
Ironically, the monk lost his immediate challenge to Kerala's land laws.
Yet his name forever protected the soul of Indian liberty.
The sharp political reaction arrived the very next morning.
On twenty-fifth April nineteen seventy-three, three senior majority judges were superseded.
A fourth-ranking judge was appointed Chief Justice of India instead.
Justices Shelat, Hegde, and Grover resigned from the bench in protest.
Despite fierce political backlash after the verdict, the basic structure doctrine survived and grew much stronger over the next four decades.
In nineteen seventy-five, in Indira Nehru Gandhi versus Raj Narain, the Court applied it to strike down an amendment shielding election disputes.
In nineteen eighty, Minerva Mills versus Union of India struck down clauses of the Forty-second Amendment that claimed unlimited parliamentary amending power.
Later, in nineteen ninety-four and two thousand seven, the Court reaffirmed secularism, federalism, and review of Ninth Schedule laws passed after nineteen seventy-three.
Today, every constitutional amendment is tested against the basic structure.
Parliament can amend the Constitution, but never erase its soul.
For law students, this case marks the triumph of constitutional supremacy.
It remains the ultimate shield of our fundamental rights.
No matter how big a parliamentary majority grows, the Constitution stands above it.
That is the enduring promise of Kesavananda Bharati.
Let us do a quick exam revision of Kesavananda Bharati versus State of Kerala, the greatest cornerstone of Indian constitutional law.
On the facts, the Edneer Mutt challenged Kerala land reforms along with the Twenty-fourth, Twenty-fifth, and Twenty-ninth Amendments before thirteen judges.
The issue was whether Article 368 had any limits; the Court overruled Golaknath, yet held seven to six that the basic structure cannot be destroyed.
The principle: Article 368 is wide but limited, and it was later cited in Indira Nehru Gandhi and Minerva Mills to protect judicial review.
